title: Days Disrupted
author: Seyward Darby
content:
The war in Iran began five months ago. Headline news about the conflict tends to focus on when and how it might end. In the meantime, the impacts of the conflict are felt worldwide—by drivers, farmers, business owners, and families. The Associated Press shares the stories of seven people suffering because of the war. Among them is Edgar Funelas, a jeepney driver in the Philippines who lives with his ten-year-old daughter:

He uses laundry soap—harsher, but cheaper—to wash his body and his clothes in the same motion, stretching what little money he has. Even before the war in Iran, he was living on the margins. A fire took their home and their belongings, forcing them to move into the brightly colored minibus he drove.

He’d hoped to be able to rent a room by now. Then diesel prices surged, and he could no longer afford the fuel to run his jeepney.

He hasn’t earned a single peso in days. There will be no breakfast. Hunger gnaws, but it’s the small rituals of privacy that he misses most: to be able to wash out of sight, to sleep behind walls, to keep his desperation from being laid bare.

title: What Would It Mean to See a New Color?
author: Brendan Fitzgerald
content:
Ready to test your knowledge of hue, value, and saturation? Rivka Galchen’s latest for The New Yorker is a trove of fascinating details about our understanding of color. Galchen opens with the buzziest tidbit: an experiment conducted by a vision scientist who used a laser to stimulate a selection of his own cone cells and glimpse a color unknown outside of his laboratory. From there, she roams—through philosophy and art history, from studios to pigment shops—complicating our understanding of perception with each new turn of her titular question.

In the children’s novel “The Midnight Fox,” by Betsy Byars, the main character daydreams about digging in his back yard and coming across a “brand-new color.” A friend of mine remembers being captivated by this scene, and trying to picture the color. “I felt like I could conceive of it, but I couldn’t see it,” she said. The eighteenth-century Scottish philosopher David Hume considered at length whether a person who had seen every shade of blue except for one would be able to picture that one un-experienced shade; he concluded that the answer was yes. In my youth, I spent an afternoon wondering if I would have been able to imagine the fluorescent yellow of highlighter markers if I’d never seen it.

title: How War Has Redefined Marriage in Gaza
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
Next to rubble and pictures of the deceased, people in Gaza are still getting married. Athar Abu Samra reports on why couples are refusing to delay their nuptials. With so much already lost, and so much still under threat, families in Gaza are seizing moments of joy wherever they can. Marriage ceremonies are no longer what they once were—nor do they express hope in quite the same way—but they have become powerful testaments to resilience.

As I worked on this story, I came to understand that the war has not only transformed weddings in Gaza. It has transformed people’s relationship with time itself. Before the war, marriage followed a familiar sequence. People finished their education, found work, built or rented a home, saved enough money and only then began planning a wedding. Families often postponed marriages until those expectations had been met. But now no one has that luxury — the luxury of time.

I spoke with one mother who had lost several of her children during the war, yet hurried to arrange the marriage of her youngest son. She told me she had always dreamed, like any mother, of watching all of her children grow up, get married, and fill her home with grandchildren. The war had taken much of that dream away, but she was determined not to lose what remained.

title: Six Teenagers, a Brutal Murder and the Story They Couldn’t Take Back
author: Brendan Fitzgerald
content:
When Jessica Black was 16 years old, she told a story to North Carolina police detectives that helped convict five friends of murder. Decades later, she’s still trying to correct the record. Matthew Bremner’s feature for Financial Times is a brisk tick-tock of efforts by Black and her incarcerated friends to overturn criminal convictions they claim were built on disturbing intimidation tactics.

The investigators do not accept these firm denials. To them, they seem likely to be the initial stories of a group of boys who know more than they are saying. As officers move in and out of interview rooms, carrying information from one interrogation to the next, the pressure intensifies. They tell the teenagers that their friends are already telling their side of it, that they should too. Under North Carolina law in 2002, police are permitted to exaggerate, even to suggest they have evidence they do not possess. There is no rule requiring a parent or other adult to be present while 14- and 15-year-olds are questioned. For most of their time in these rooms, the five boys are alone. When I interviewed him in late 2025, Tolliver told me that a detective asked him to hold out his arm. “That’s the vein,” he told him. “This is where the lethal injection would go.”

title: What Is It Like to Be a Cucumber?
author: Peter Rubin
content:
I’d be lying if I said I understand everything Michael Levin believes. But I’m also not alone; sometimes his own colleagues can’t even follow his arguments. Elizabeth Weil’s profile of the renegade (and genius) biologist bridges that gap, sketching out Levin’s research and claims in a way that’s just grokkable enough to blow your mind. I mean this as a true compliment: When’s the last time we had a genuine mad scientist on our hands?

Critics accuse Levin of all kinds of teleological crimes — making unfalsifiable claims, using words in ways that render those words meaningless. Levin is unfazed. In his talks, he tries to disarm his detractors by preempting the accusation that he’s nuts: “I have some unusual things to say and then I have some crazy things to say”; “So this is a kind of crazy claim I’m making.” His true retort is his wet lab. There, at the bench, he’s working to prove his metaphysics by running old-school (in a way) biological experiments. He studies flatworms with two heads. Frogs with eyes on their stomachs. Little round creatures called xenobots, synthesized from frog skin cells. They swim like tiny Pac-Men. They do not exist in nature.

“The only thing that ever settles arguments is technology,” Levin tells me, a line he borrowed from biophysicist Chris Fields. “People have been saying for thousands of years what they think” about minds, consciousness, souls, energy fields. “What I can contribute is ways to test some of those things.”

title: Critics’ Cult Classics: Hanif Abdurraqib on Camp Lo’s “Uptown Saturday Night”
author: @NewYorker
content:
The 1997 album marked a crossroads for hip-hop, as the genre was being torn between elaborate mythmaking and a kind of true crime.

August 6, 2026

Download a transcript.

Listen and subscribe: Apple | Spotify | Wherever You Listen

Sign up to receive our weekly cultural-recommendations newsletter.

When it dropped in January of 1997, Camp Lo’s “Uptown Saturday Night” thrilled some listeners and confounded others. In the first in a series of Critics at Large interview episodes devoted to resurfacing beloved cult classics, Vinson Cunningham talks with Hanif Abdurraqib, a contributing writer for The New Yorker and a diehard fan of the Camp Lo project. Abdurraqib describes “Uptown Saturday Night,” which leaned on Blaxploitation tropes to paint a strikingly cinematic picture of New York City, as “essentially a heist film” unto itself. Together, they discuss the album’s lukewarm reception at the time, and why its creative approach to storytelling seemed to land on deaf ears. One explanation is that the hip-hop marketplace of the era was increasingly demanding that musicians pick a lane: underground or mainstream, socially conscious or unapologetically opulent. “ ‘Uptown Saturday Night’ got lost in that because it didn’t really have a foothold in either world,” Abdurraqib says. “At a time when a lot of these guys with underground roots were bending to the hyper-commercialization of hip-hop, Camp Lo never changed who they were.”

title: How Jordan Harper Reinvented Noir for the Epstein Era
author: @NewYorker
content:
This year’s buzzy “A Violent Masterpiece” inverts the genre’s traditional contrast between optimism and despair. Is a hopeful crime novel still a noir?

August 5, 2026

Illustration by Clay Rodery

As I approached the end of Jordan Harper’s “A Violent Masterpiece,” this year’s buzzy crime novel, I was surprised—slightly disoriented, even—by the presence of an unexpected feeling on the page: hope. The feeling is unexpected because of all that has come before it, including in “Everybody Knows,” Harper’s previous novel, to which “A Violent Masterpiece” is a sequel of sorts (though perfectly readable on its own). The world of these books is a bleak, fallen one: a grotesque, Day-Glo Los Angeles where the rich and powerful do whatever they want, aided by armies of flunkies and stacks of N.D.A.s. Both stories burst at the seams with corrupt cops and politicians, private mercenaries, concierge peddlers of drugs and sex and plastic surgery, lawyers who stop charges from sticking, and “black-bag publicists” who stop dirt from surfacing. One central character is a monster clearly cobbled together from recent-ish headlines of American depravity: part Weinstein, part Epstein. (In “A Violent Masterpiece,” he quickly winds up dead in jail.) The novels’ Boschian background is full of people whom the powerful no longer have any need for, or never cared about in the first place—discarded child actors, assistants who couldn’t hack it, addicts who live in encampments.

Harper has been widely fêted by both critics and his fellow crime writers. (“Everybody Knows” was, according to the detective novelist Michael Connelly, “the book everybody’s been waiting for.”) When “A Violent Masterpiece” came out, in April, the Times Book Review dubbed it “the noir novel for our times.” In the noir tradition, Harper’s writing trains us not to set our hopes too high. Again and again, he shows us how would-be rebels who fight “the Beast” (as a few of them call L.A.’s power structure) get defeated and punished, often violently. His prose radiates an ecstatic pessimism, as if lit up from within by the relief of not having to sugarcoat things with comforting lies. “This wicked truth that moves under everything rises to the surface,” he writes, describing an outbreak of police violence against protesters. “The serpent that circles the world shows itself.”

But, as the new book hurtles toward its climax, it starts to seem as if at least some of Harper’s characters might eke out some kind of victory against the Beast. Is Harper, like so many noir writers before him, raising our hopes for the express purpose of dashing them against the rocks? Or is hope really in reach? If so, what kind?

“Noir,” a term originally coined by French critics to refer to certain American films made in the nineteen-forties, now refers to all manner of stories, onscreen and off, with a wide variety of preoccupations and stylistic tendencies. If there’s a single unifying fixation, it might be the contrast between surface and reality, and especially between superficially happy cover stories and subterranean despair. In the forties and fifties, noir stories of criminality thumbed their noses—with style—at the enforced cheeriness of postwar American life, dissenting from the era’s sunny master narrative: that the U.S. was always and forever a beacon of progress, an unambiguous force for good in the world, a place where hard work and upstanding behavior were always rewarded, and crime never paid. In the decades since, more recent variants have adapted this schema for other settings. West Coast noir insists that the sun-drenched beauty and free-spirit mythology of California hide a world of corruption and greed. Nordic noir suggests the presence of violence and hatred beneath the tranquillity and order of the Scandinavian welfare state, just as Southern noir peels back hospitality and charm to reveal repressed family secrets and moral decay.

Noir always means darkness—but how much of it, and how completely, in “true” noir, it blots out the sun has always been a debate among connoisseurs. In essays accompanying their co-edited anthology, “The Best American Noir of the Century,” published in 2010, the genre masters James Ellroy and Otto Penzler insist that literary noir has to mean total bleakness: stories exclusively about desperate people doomed to lose it all, because them’s the breaks. The genre, Ellroy writes, is “the nightmare of flawed souls with big dreams and the precise how and why of the all-time sure thing that goes bad. Noir is opportunity as fatality, social justice as sanctified shuck, and sexual love as a one-way ticket to hell.”

Harper is a well-known fan of Ellroy’s; he spent years working up a TV adaptation (never picked up by CBS) of Ellroy’s 1997 novel, “L.A. Confidential,” and, in the afterword for “A Violent Masterpiece,” he thanks Ellroy “for carving the path.” So, as expected, he has gloom to spare. His books are pervaded by depravity of all sorts: casting agencies that funnel desperate young actors to powerful older men; little Weinsteins everywhere; rich kids who get off on launching explosives in homeless camps. There’s even a human-tissue business that scouts the morgue, looking for corpses to process into the stuff of butt lifts and plumped lips. If you’re thinking that a human-tissue business sounds like a great way to hide evidence, you’ve probably been reading too much noir; you’re also right.

“A Violent Masterpiece” alternates between the perspectives of three characters. None of them lose their innocence in the course of the story; they lost it long ago. (Ellroy again: “America was never innocent. We popped our cherry on the boat over and looked back with no regrets.”) Kara Delgado works as a fixer at L.A.’s premier concierge service, catering to the outré tastes and perversions of the city’s élite. Doug Gibson, the novel’s closest thing to an idealist, is a pugilistic criminal-defense lawyer, the kind with ads on bus-stop benches. He has a well-worn speech about the value of due process and can speak trenchantly about all the ways the system is stacked against his clients. But somewhere inside he knows that the status quo has made him a wealthy man, while he hasn’t changed the status quo a bit. Jake Deal, formerly employed to dig up secrets for a gossip website, now works for himself as a live streamer; he drives through the city, using a police scanner to track down scenes of chaos and carnage, feeding his viewers’ appetite for vérité gore. If the photos are good enough, he can sell them to his old employer.

All three characters know exactly what’s wrong with the world. If they were in the mood, they could articulate a cogent critique (and, in the next breath, a plausible minimization) of their own contribution. All three are shown enjoying what they do, at least some of the time. Each, in a way, gets to be up close to the gears that make the real world turn. Each gets to enjoy the adrenaline rush of making the world bend to his or her will, at least a little bit: Kara when she gets every rule rendered moot on her clients’ behalf; Gibson when he gets his clients out, or their sentences reduced; Jake when he gets the right footage or finds the right words for his live stream (called the Creepy Crawl) and sees his followers go wild. Here he is, talking to his audience:

“We are America dreaming itself. We’re a fractal of fortunes and crimes, fortunes and crimes. We’re cars and guns and land grabs and tacos, money and movies and big tits and death, all served under a dirty sky—please rise for our national anthem, am I right?”

He picks up speed. The light turns red. He rockets through it. Pissed-off horns chorus on both sides. He glances down at the chat, watching it roll with HELL YEAHs and mushroom-cloud animations. He turns hard onto Florence—tires sing. This high, wild laugh comes out of him.

In interviews, Harper has described prepping for the novel by driving around L.A. Jake-style, police scanner and all. The live streamer feels like a stand-in for the author’s own ambivalence about crime writing. In one charged scene, Jake—moonlighting as an investigator for a celebrity-blackmail outfit—films through a window as a famous actor becomes increasingly violent with a woman he’s just picked up. At first, Jake is worried mostly about the poor quality of the video he’s capturing. But the worse the scene unfolding through the glass gets, the more troubled Jake becomes—by the celebrity’s actions, yes, but also by his own. Almost by reflex, he punches the window, smashing it. The intensity of Harper’s writing, especially in his grisliest depictions of violence, can feel like the prose equivalent of trying to smash the glass. At other times, the book embodies an awareness that glass-smashing isn’t in the cards.

What is the line, you can sense Harper asking, between documenting the horrors of the world and profiting from them, packaging them—like Jake, like Harper, like almost all crime writers—for an audience safe at home? In one of the novel’s eeriest moments, Jake is driving around the city, talking into his microphone, as usual—only now it’s intentionally unplugged and he isn’t live-streaming, because what he’s up to (fighting the Beast) is secret. He’s trying, I think, to figure out what he sounds like when just describing the world isn’t enough, and when he’s not putting his description up for sale. It’s as if Harper, too, is trying to figure out what kind of noir he’s really writing, and why.

Around the novel’s halfway point, one of Harper’s characters dares to change, or try changing, his relationship to the Beast. They receive a brutal noir comeuppance, in a scene of terrifying violence. Reading it, I felt that trademark quicksand feeling of the most hard-core noirs: that every action, no matter its intentions, is sending its characters in only one direction—down, closer to the heart of darkness.

But then the book keeps going. If your preferred experience of reading crime fiction relies on knowing absolutely nothing about how things pan out, stop here. Harper’s characters live to fight another day. (Well, some of them do.) More than that, though, they transform into people who are resolved to fight, with new weapons in their arsenals and new feelings in their hearts. “I’m thinking, maybe there’s another way of being,” one of them says fumblingly, in a rare moment of direct sincerity. “I’d like to find out if there is.”

Is this still noir? Partisans of the Ellroy and Penzler definition probably wouldn’t say so, except perhaps as a diss, proof of a contemporary inability to face misery without slapping on some good cheer at the end. Or perhaps one might say: It’s not really noir—and that’s fine! Ellroy himself, in the nineteen-nineties, declared, “Noir is dead for me,” because its world view was too simple, and left no room for him to explore subjects such as love, redemption, and self-knowledge without forcing them into a predetermined script.

But there’s another way of looking at the noir-ness of Harper’s writing, one that draws on the genre’s history without using it as the basis for an essentialist definition. If traditional noir drew much of its energy from sneering with style at America’s sunny master narratives, those narratives have largely broken down, as has the homogenous mass-media ecosystem that endlessly recirculated them. There’s no significant cultural prohibition against pointing out that things aren’t going so well. (“Things Aren’t Going So Well” is easy to imagine as the title of a Times op-ed, a viral Substack post, or a new A24 movie.) In the era of Trump, Epstein, and all the tentacular corruption they represent, pointing out that there’s rot beneath the surface, or a repressed truth behind the smile, isn’t edgy; it’s rote. Now the rot is right there on the surface; the people smiling are less likely to be clueless optimists than the people who are happy about the rot, or profiting from it. A network of particularly depraved men in “A Violent Masterpiece” has a name for itself, one that speaks not just to its members’ impunity but also to their delight: the Kids in the Candy Store.

Maybe it makes sense that a noir for our current era would dare to find its way to hope, albeit hope of a very noirish variety. If Harper’s voracious hunger for piling on details of Hollywood depravity can seem exploitative, the noir framework suggests another way of looking at it. In order to point—against the prevailing mood of our times—toward a sliver of optimism, he needs his readers to know, beyond the shadow of a doubt, that he’s fully aware just how hard that optimism is to find. The risk, of course, is that he makes the depravity so convincing that hope can only pale in comparison. Readers will have to decide for themselves what to believe. Doing so will mean asking just what they think about the world today and our prospects within it. These are questions that can be discomfiting, even disturbing. Which is, in its way, pretty noir. ♦

title: Why the Democratic Establishment Can’t Win Over Young Voters
author: @NewYorker
content:
One of the most thought-provoking books I’ve read in the past year is Noam Scheiber’s “Mutiny: The Rise and Revolt of the College-Educated Working Class.” Scheiber presents a series of incisively reported profiles of young people who did everything they were asked to do but still found themselves working at a Starbucks or in an Amazon warehouse. Their discontent, Scheiber concludes, isn’t explicitly economic or cultural or political but, rather, is what happens when people with degrees realize that what they thought was a temporary postgraduate job will almost certainly become their career. There is no dream job coming; the bridge is the road and the final destination. Combine that realization with the harsh reality of retail jobs, plus a revival of class solidarity and labor politics—thanks, in part, to Bernie Sanders—and the result is a highly educated and credentialled political movement that has swept leftist candidates into office across the country.

This new voting bloc has two similar but distinct components. There are what I call the Subaru Socialists: college-educated millennials in their thirties and early forties who earn a somewhat steady income but not what they expected. These voters arrived at their politics via the Great Recession, Occupy Wall Street, and the continual escalation of housing prices in urban areas—all of which heightened the contrast between what they were promised when they took on student debt and their current circumstances. Then there are the Great Disappointed, a younger set. They don’t have strong memories of the 2008 financial crash, as their millennial elders do, but they came of age during the pandemic and saw that seemingly invincible institutions could, in fact, sputter and fail when placed under duress. Like the Subaru Socialists, these twenty-two-to-thirty-year-olds aren’t exactly happy with the return on their educational investment. But their political views have seemingly coalesced less around the economy than around the war in Gaza, which serves as a character test for any politician who asks for their vote.

Pundits have many things to say about Subaru Socialists and the Great Disappointed, and almost all of it is at least partially true. Given that these voters are mostly white college graduates between the ages of twenty-five and forty, they are indeed “privileged” in the most boring sense of that word. They probably do spend a lot of time online. Many of them live in historically Black or immigrant neighborhoods where rent is cheaper, at least until enough of them move in and start opening coffee shops that play Stereolab or whatever. Economically, they might not be particularly worse off than their boomer parents were at the same point in their lives. They vote at a high rate for their age, which is why they need to be taken seriously.

Many skeptics see a contradiction in high-achieving, mostly white young voters employing rhetoric about labor and solidarity. Every big Election Night for the leftists comes with the same eye-rolling complaint from centrists and the right: “Oh, great, some gentrifiers who went to Sarah Lawrence are cosplaying socialism and pretending they’re working class.” But all voting blocs come with some supposed contradictions; poor, non-college-educated voters regularly prefer candidates who support tax cuts for billionaires, for example. What this usually means is that the apparent contradiction isn’t particularly relevant for those voters or very revealing about their preferences. And a whole lot of people under the age of forty-five no longer believe that indicators such as wages, unemployment, or the number of college degrees that are handed out in a given year have much to do with a healthy economy. They are concerned with the consolidation of wealth, the price of housing, the cost of child care, and student debt. And, absent an upheaval of the entire political establishment in this country, they don’t really see why anything would get better, even if they might admit that things are not so bad for them personally right now.

There’s another term for people who make an O.K. salary at a normal job but sometimes struggle to afford housing and child care: the middle class. No term in American politics is quite as slippery or misshapen. I imagine that the majority of Subaru Socialists in their thirties would resist the label, even if they make the median household income for their neighborhood and work a steady job that allows them to put away a modest amount of money each month in a retirement account. This resistance comes from a variety of sources, but it’s largely cultural: “middle class” suggests cul-de-sacs in the suburbs, moderate politics, and a career. The manager of a Starbucks or an enterprising but disgruntled gig-economy worker might pull down enough money to land in the middle class, but they will not feel the homogenizing stability and somewhat stultifying comfort they likely associate with the phrase.

During one of the many iterations of her Presidential campaign, Kamala Harris started talking about something she called an “opportunity economy” that would lift the “middle class” out of despair. I recall thinking that I had no idea who she meant by the middle class: was she talking about postal workers and teachers in the Midwest whose communities had been ravaged by opioids and deindustrialization? Was she talking about nurses in New Jersey who were being priced out of their homes?

Harris was probably trying to talk to Subaru Socialists and the Great Disappointed. Her policy proposals during the “middle-class” phase of her campaign involved federal assistance on down payments for a first home, child tax credits for parents of newborns, and help if you wanted to start a small business. They might have benefitted someone living in the suburbs of Detroit, for instance—someone who graduated from Michigan State, say, and cobbles together about sixty-five thousand dollars a year through a retail job and Uber driving but dreams of opening her own coffee shop and starting a family. If that person heard Harris talking about “the middle class,” would she have assumed that Harris was talking about her?

The inability to imagine a middle-class life—especially for the Subaru Socialists right on the cusp of comfort—seems to be what’s behind a slate of recent electoral victories for the Democratic Socialists of America. In a recent post on his Substack, Nate Silver analyzed data from the Cooperative Election Study and found that the group of people most likely to vote Democratic were postgraduate-degree holders who had a household income between thirty thousand and sixty thousand dollars. Much of the membership of the Democratic Socialists of America, Silver pointed out, sat squarely within that band: more than eighty per cent of the members above the age of twenty-four had a bachelor’s degree, and forty-five per cent of all respondents lived in households earning less than sixty thousand dollars a year. (Silver found that, according to C.E.S. data, only about nineteen per cent of all college graduates in America make that little.) A profile emerges of the typical D.S.A. member, and it resembles our hopeful future coffee-shop owner: a college-educated voter in her early thirties who isn’t making as much as she thought she would.

Harris was correct to include this person in the middle class, even if this person might not see it that way. The problem for the Democratic establishment is that the Subaru Socialist does not believe that Harris and those like her have any interest in helping her out, even if they advance a slate of proposals that will undeniably get her closer to opening that coffee shop and starting that family. This helps to explain why the Biden Administration gets so little credit from the left for an economic policy drafted by former Elizabeth Warren staffers, or why nobody seems to care that Lina Khan, who currently chairs the board of the New York City Economic Development Corporation under Zohran Mamdani, actually held a much more important position under Biden. Absent a truly transformative and well-marketed idea such as universal health care, there’s nothing an establishment candidate can do to satisfy the Subaru Socialists, because the bad deal they were sold as children—study, go to college, and you’ll find yourself in a better place than your parents—has led to a fundamental discontentment with the way things are.

The Subaru Socialists and the Great Disappointed are certainly aligned in much of their politics, but their motivations, I believe, aren’t exactly the same. Last week, on the podcast I host, the pollster Adam Carlson said that he was seeing evidence that age, even more than educational attainment, was the most reliable indicator of how a person would vote in a Democratic primary. Age, he said, was “the single biggest determinant in how someone would vote in the June New York City primaries,” for instance. And in Michigan, he noted, a generation gap had begun to open up within the Black electorate—recent reporting showed that older voters preferred the establishment candidate, Haley Stevens, and younger voters were more likely to support the progressive Abdul El-Sayed. On the broader stage of general elections, Carlson argued, “Gen Z voters are less loyal to a party and are more elastic and seemingly want to punish whatever party is in power when things are bad for them.”

This anti-establishment rebellion has coalesced around Gaza. A majority of young Democrats believe that their tax dollars are funding a genocide; candidates like Melat Kiros, who defeated the longtime Colorado congresswoman Diana DeGette in a primary, are running to the left of progressive incumbents not so much on economic issues as in their condemnation of Israel and of America’s continued military aid to the country. Gaza has become a litmus test for anti-establishment voters on both the left and the right—if you take a dime from AIPAC or if you aren’t the most fervently anti-Israel candidate in the field, you will have a tough time winning a Democratic seat in an urban, highly educated blue district.

The future of the Democratic Party involves a synthesis of Subaru Socialism’s disillusionment with the American promise and the polarized, hard-line moralizing of Gen Z. Young voters aren’t the only angry ones, of course; older Democrats are still understandably furious at a party that lost to Donald Trump twice and seems to have done precious little to stand in his way during the past year and a half. But it’s younger voters who have begun to give a political form and shape to that reactionary anger. You could look at the platforms of their favorite politicians and label that form “economic populism,” but I think that’s an imperfect assessment—what matters isn’t so much the specific policies but rather the promise of upheaval.

Given the robust turnout of this new voting bloc in high-profile elections, plus the press’s fascination with these voters—there are many Subaru Socialists in the media’s ranks, including me—the Democratic Party will almost certainly remake itself in the image of Mamdani, Kiros, El-Sayed, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Francesca Hong, who looks poised to win the Democratic nomination for governor of Wisconsin. Politics, after all, is largely a copycat game. And what, at this point, is the alternative? ♦

title: New extraction shooter BR1 Infinite brings new meaning to "pay to play" by paying players for each in-game kill
author: Vikki Blake
content:
Pay to slay.

New extraction shooter, BR1 Infinite, is reportedly bringing new meaning to the term "pay to play" by paying players for each in-game kill.

As spotted by Polygon, BR1 Infinite is offering players $10 (£7.41) an hour and $1 (75p) for every kill. The catch, however, is that spawning into a match costs $1 of your IRL hard-earned cash, so a bad run can damage your bank balance as well as your pride.

BR1 Infinite bills itself as the first real-money extraction shooter developed by Bravo Ready Studios, a company with a background steeped in gambling and consumer tech. It's reportedly backed by PUBG publisher Krafton, Solana Ventures and 6MV, among other investors.

Access is invite-only and PC-only, with a limited number of spots advertised in each post.

Once in, the monetisation loop revolves around keeping a positive kill/death ratio, looting and extracting cash drops, and trading operatives and skins. The team claims to have paid out more than $100,000 to testers so far, who reportedly get free spawns as part of that arrangement.

Beyond the concerns about legitimacy and safety, some players think a real-money system like this is also an open invitation to cheating, boosting, and exploits, all layered on top of what's reportedly a fairly bare-bones shooter, with players controlling droids or apes across simple maps in pursuit of the payouts. That hasn't stopped 40,000 players joining the Discord, though.

More concerningly still, there doesn't seem to be any obvious age gate or verification to prevent underage players from accessing a game that contains pay-to-win-like mechanics.

Curiously, the company's social presence goes back much further than the game itself. One profile dates to 2011 and has undergone seven name changes, the most recent in 2022, around the time Bravo Ready Studios began releasing games in earnest (thanks, IG). It's unclear exactly why BR1 Infinite has only started trending now, though scepticism about the project dates back a couple of years online.

title: New Survey Data on Public Perceptions of the Supreme Court
author: IlyaSomin
content:
Back in May, I wrote about survey data indicating a modest boost in the Supreme Court's popularity with the public, possibly caused by its February decision in the tariff case (which I helped litigate). Since then, the Supreme Court has issued its major decisions in a large number of cases, including those on birthright citizenship, the Second Amendment, executive removal power, and more. Recently, Marquette Law School came out with a new poll assessing public perceptions of the Court in the wake of those rulings. It finds that the Court as a whole remains modestly unpopular (47% approve, 53% disapprove), but that most of its major recent decisions have majority public support. The Court also remains a bit more popular than just before the tariff ruling, and much more popular than the other two branches of government. There are other interesting findings, as well, including on perceptions of individual justices (about which most of the public is generally ignorant).

As discussed below, the Marquette survey has a few unfortunate methodological problems. But it nonetheless provides some useful information about public perceptions of the Court.

Before going on, I will emphasize, yet again, that the Court's popularity (or lack thereof) says little about the quality of its decisions. Survey data consistently shows that most Americans know very little about the Constitution and the Court's work, and a majority of the public cannot even name one Supreme Court justice and know little about them (the Marquette poll further confirms this latter point). I also do not claim that majority public support for decisions I like (including the tariff ruling!) "proves" those decisions are correct. It does not. But, for reasons to be discussed below, public opinion about the Court does matter, in so far as it is important to protecting the institution of judicial review against potential attacks from both the right and the left. It may also be of interest to students of the Court and students of public opinion (I happen to be both).

The Court's 47% approval rating is slightly higher than the 44% it got in the same poll in mid to late 2025, and about the same as the 46% it got in May (after the tariff case, but before the other rulings). An April Marquette poll showed 42% approval. This is consistent with other survey data indicating a slight improvement in early 2026, possibly driven by the tariff decision. Though the Marquette poll shows more stability than some of the others, and fluctuations between 42 and 47 could just be due to random variation.

The Court also remains much more popular (or, rather, much less unpopular) than the other two branches of government. The Marquette survey finds that President Trump has only a 38% favorability rating (a whopping 60% view him unfavorably), and both congressional Republicans and congressional Democrats, are also highly unpopular, probably even more so than Trump. The same goes for the Republican and Democratic parties generally. This, too, is consistent with previous polls showing that public views of the Court are more favorable than those of the other two branches of government.

Marquette also surveyed public attitudes on 13 significant decisions made by the Court within the last year. And all but two command majority support, including many supported by large majorities:

The tariff case (66% support), allowing states to ban transgender athletes from women's sports (65%), and Trump v. Cook - the decision protecting the autonomy of the Federal Reserve Board (70%) are all highly popular. Louisiana v. Callais - the Voting Rights Act decision that attracted strong left-wing ire - enjoys modest majority support (53%).  The only two decisions surveyed that don't have majority support are Trump v. Slaughter (ruling that the president can remove the heads of most other independent agencies), and a ruling allowing parties to coordinate campaign expenditures with campaigns. And even those two decisions are only modestly unpopular, getting support from 49% of the public, and 47% respectively.

These results suggest that the Court's majority this year was very much not out of step with public opinion, as critics sometimes charge. I say that even though I myself am not a fan of some of the decisions the public agrees with. While I agree with part of the reasoning of Callais, I worry that the Court's approach creates way too much leeway for racial gerrymandering by Republicans. I also have significant reservations about Trump v. Slaughter and its relationship to Trump v. Cook; reconciling those two decisions is difficult to say the least.

There are a few methodological issues with this part of the Marquette survey. The survey's descriptions of the rulings in the questions are fairly detailed and precise. But that very fact might make them hard to understand for respondents who don't know much about the issues involved (which is likely to be a large proportion of them). In addition, all of these questions are structured as "forced choice" questions, on which respondents do not have the option of answering "don't know" or "no opinion." That means the survey is capturing a lot of responses by people who don't actually have meaningful opinions on the case in question.

In addition, the Court included one case it probably should not have, and omitted at least one that should have been included. The Court did not really rule on E. Jean Carroll's suit against Trump. As the Marquette survey notes, it merely refused to review the lower court decision in favor of Carroll.  This is not actually a precedent-setting decision by the Court, and not that significant for anyone but Trump and Carroll. By contrast, the survey wrongly omits the Court's terrible decision in the Haitian TPS case, which will both have a massive immediate impact on hundreds of thousands of people and set a bad precedent for future executive immigration policies motivated by racial and ethnic prejudice.

Despite these caveats, it is clear that most of the Court's recent major decisions enjoy majority public support, some overwhelmingly so. And none are highly unpopular.

Marquette also surveyed public opinion about individual justices:

Strikingly - but not surprisingly  - Clarence Thomas is the only justice about whom a majority of respondents say they know enough to have an opinion. That's likely because of a combination of his long tenure, his highly controversial confirmation hearings (which many older respondents may remember), and his being the only Black justice during most of his tenure (until Ketanji Brown Jackson was confirmed in 2022).

The fact that most Americans say they haven't heard enough to have an opinion of most of the justices (including even Chief Justice John Roberts) is a further indication of widespread public ignorance about the Court and its work. I would add that we should not assume that those who do express an opinion are actually knowledgeable. Studies show that many survey respondents are willing to express views about people and issues they know little about, rather than admit ignorance. Thus, classic surveys show that large numbers of respondents will express opinions about entirely fictional legislation, such as the "Metallic Metals Act." A 2015 poll found that 30% of Republicans and 19% of Democrats supported bombing the nation of Agrabah (which is actually a fictional entity from the Disney movie Aladdin), rather than admitting they had no opinion or didn't know about it.

A recent YouGov poll, which I analyzed in my last post on the Supreme Court and public opinion, found higher percentages willing to an express an opinion about the justices. Only 27% said they had "no opinion" about Thomas, while the "no opinion" percentages for the others ranged from 35% to 44%. The key difference between this poll and the Marquette one is that YouGov gave respondents the option of saying they had "slightly" or "very" favorable or unfavorable views, instead of just allowing "favorable" or "unfavorable" (as Marquette did). I suspect many respondents who know little or nothing about the justices were willing to pick "slighly favorable" or "slightly unfavorable" in the YouGov poll, but many such people (in the Marquette survey) were unwilling to express a stronger, more unqualified view.

In both the Marquette survey and YouGov, the liberal justices are more popular than the conservative ones, and the single most popular justice in both surveys is  Sonia Sotomayor (29% favorable vs. 19% unfavorable in Marquette; 38-27 in YouGov). This may be because more of the public prefers liberal jurisprudence. But that conjecture is belied by surveys on specific decisions, where many conservative (though, of course, not all) rulings are popular (e.g. - striking down affirmative action policies).

I suspect the bigger factor here is the growing "diploma divide" in American politics. Education is increasingly correlated with support for Democrats, while the Republicans get most of their support from the least-educated parts of the population. Education is also highly correlated with political knowledge. Thus, the kinds of people who have at least some substantial knowledge of the Supreme Court justices are disproportionately likely to be liberal Democrats. On the other hand, those willing to admit they don't know enough to have an opinion are disproportionately conservative Republicans.

It's worth noting that none of the justices are wildly unpopular. Even Clarence Thomas - the single most negatively rated justice in both the Marquette and YouGov polls - has only modestly negative approval ratings (-3 in Marquette, and -9 in YouGov). Trump and Congress would love to have approval ratings like that!

Overall, the Court is only modestly unpopular, and its major recent rulings mostly get more support than opposition from the public.

As already noted, this does not prove the Court is doing a good job, either in general or on any specific case. But it is significant, nonetheless.

Today, judicial review faces potential threats from both right and left. Trump and many of his supporters have flirted with the idea of disobeying judicial rulings that go against them, and have at times flouted various lower-court rulings or tried to deceive judges. On the left, there is renewed momentum for undermining judicial review through court-packing (which I documented and criticized here and here). To the extent that the Court and its decisions remain more popular (or at least less unpopular) than the other branches of government, it makes it harder for either right or left to undermine judicial review.

I am far from an unequivocal cheerleader for the Court and its current majority. I think they have gotten some important issues badly wrong, including the Haitian TPS immigration case and the Pung property rights case, just last month. Nonetheless, I think we are far better off with strong judicial review than without it, and that the judiciary is - on the whole - doing its job far better than either Congress or the executive branch right now. For these reasons, I hope the Court can maintain its relative popularity and - ideally - boost it further, at least somewhat.

I would not want the justices to prioritize popularity too much. If the Court became wildly popular, I would worry they aren't doing enough to protect the rights of unpopular minorities, or to enforce constitutional constraints on government power in situations where politicians pursue popular-but-illegal and dangerous policies. In an ideal world, the Court's popularity would be totally irrelevant, except perhaps as a subject for academic research. But we don't live in that ideal world. Far from it.
